01 / 02  ·  Business intelligence · Operations

Power BI · Staffing optimiser · Live

A staffing optimiser for café managers

Cafés run on thin margins, and payroll is the biggest cost a manager actually controls — so matching staff to real demand, hour by hour and season by season, is what keeps the business in profit. This dashboard turns a café's point-of-sale log into exactly that decision.

Open live dashboard Opens the interactive report via Power BI Publish to web.

The build

Built in Power BI from the point-of-sale transaction log. Custom DAX measures turn raw orders into demand curves per 15-minute slot, a barista-workload index, and category breakdowns — with month and weekday filters so a manager can slice the view to any day or season.

Power BIDAX measuresdemand forecastingcost optimisation

Why it matters

  • Payroll is the biggest cost a manager controls. On thin café margins, overstaffing a quiet hour can wipe out a shift's profit — so the win is matching people to demand, not guessing at it.
  • Demand concentrates in the 8–11 AM rush — nearly double the midday rate. Staff the peak, trim the quiet midday and evening tails, and the schedule starts paying for itself.
  • Month and weekday filters make it a planning tool. A Saturday in July is staffed differently from a rainy Tuesday in February — the manager decides with data, not instinct.

The build

A fully interactive Looker Studio dashboard — cross-filtering maps, funding breakdowns, tech-hub tiers and capital-efficiency measures across economies. Calculated fields for capital efficiency (valuation ÷ raised) and burn velocity let the views compare how well each market turns money into value.

Looker Studiocalculated fieldsgeospatialdata modelling

What the data says

  • Estonia — value beyond its size. A tier-3 hub whose total startup value exceeds its entire GDP by 60%.
  • Capital follows geography, not merit. South Korea outranks the Netherlands on ecosystem quality yet attracts far less funding.
  • The US isn't the best allocator. Despite dominating VC flows, it underperforms on capital efficiency and burn rate.
  • Tier-4 hubs punch above their weight — just 1.4% of invested capital, but 5.7% of value created.

01 / 03  ·  Econometrics · Market intelligence

OLS Regression · Python · Power BI

What actually moves the European steel price

A cost-side regression on eleven years of monthly data — asking which raw-material and energy costs move hot-rolled band steel, and, just as importantly, which don't.

0.38
Scrap elasticity — nearly 3× iron ore's 0.13
~34%
of monthly price moves explained by raw-material costs
138
monthly observations, 2015–2026
2 / 4
drivers statistically significant & robust

The method

Multiple linear regression (OLS) on monthly log-changes — chosen to avoid spurious trend correlation and to read coefficients directly as elasticities. Significance was confirmed with autocorrelation-robust Newey–West standard errors.

statsmodelsNewey–West SElog-change OLSelasticity

What I found

  • Scrap is the strongest driver. A 1% move in scrap is associated with a 0.38% move in steel — nearly triple iron ore's 0.13%. That fits Europe's scrap-heavy, electric-arc-furnace production.
  • Both effects are significant and robust — very unlikely to be chance, and they hold after correcting for autocorrelation.
  • Natural gas and EU carbon are not significant in the short run — both were tested and kept as controls, but neither measurably moves the price.
Data: worldbank.org · steelbenchmarker.com · tradingeconomics.com  ·  Monthly 01/2015 – 06/2026
02 / 03  ·  Data storytelling · Python

Matplotlib · Learning-curve analysis · LinkedIn

Why solar got 99.8% cheaper

A watt of solar cost about $128 in 1975 and roughly 26 cents today. I broke the decline down by decade, then plotted it against how much solar the world had built — to find out what actually drove it.

−99.8%
price per watt, 1975 → 2024
R²=0.95
price-vs-cumulative-capacity fit
−27%
price for every doubling of installed capacity
6
policy milestones mapped to the curve

The approach

Four linked matplotlib figures on a shared visual system: the long decline on a log scale, the drop decomposed by decade, a log–log fit of price against cumulative capacity, and the same curve annotated with the policies behind each doubling.

pandasmatplotliblog–log fitannotation design

What stood out

  • It fell every single decade — but not evenly: ~87% in the first ten years, slower through the 1990s, then another 84% in the 2000s manufacturing boom.
  • A textbook learning curve. Plot price against capacity and it's almost a straight line — each doubling cut cost by ~27%.
  • The doublings weren't automatic. Oil-shock R&D, Japanese and German rooftop subsidies, feed-in tariffs, and China's scale-up all created the demand that drove costs down.
Data: Our World in Data — IRENA · Nemet (2009) · Farmer & Lafond (2016) View on LinkedIn
03 / 03  ·  Data storytelling · Python

Pandas · Index construction · LinkedIn

What a Norwegian salary actually buys

Since 1979, Norwegian pay rose 847% and prices 432% — which sounds like a clean success story. It's half of one, because "prices" leaves out housing. So I measured the same salary against three different markets.

+78%
real purchasing power vs. 1979 (a record high in 2025)
7 / 46
years real pay actually fell
+339%
house prices since 1999 — vs wages +170%
+43 / −39
% more everyday goods, but % less housing

The approach

Wage, CPI, housing and exchange-rate series rebased to common index years, then recombined into a single measure: what one year's average salary actually buys in each market. The reframing — purchasing power, not headline growth — is what turns one number into three honest answers.

pandasindex rebasingreal vs nominalmatplotlib

Same salary, three stories

  • Pay outran the CPI for 46 years — real wages are up 78%, and dips were rare (just 7 years, including the 2022–23 squeeze).
  • But housing ran far ahead of pay. House prices are up 339% since 1999 while wages rose 170%.
  • So purchasing power depends on what you measure against: the same salary buys 43% more everyday goods, 11% more abroad — and 39% less housing.
Data: Statistics Norway (SSB) · Norges Bank · Eurostat View on LinkedIn
